q: Which compound can form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules?
h: Molecules H-bond with each other only if an H is attached directly to F, N or O.
w: Ethylamine has N–H bonds, so it H-bonds with itself: CH3CH2NH2. In dimethyl ether, trimethylamine and fluoroethane every H is on carbon, so there is no H–F, H–N or H–O to donate.

q: Which compound cannot hydrogen bond with other molecules of itself but can accept hydrogen bonds from water, making it partly water-soluble?
h: Look for an O atom with lone pairs but no H on O, N or F.
w: Diethyl ether has an O that water's H can bond to, but no O–H of its own: CH3CH2OCH2CH3. 1-Butanol and propanoic acid have O–H and H-bond with themselves; pentane has no O at all.

q: Which compound has the lowest boiling point?
h: All are nonpolar alkanes. More carbons raise the boiling point; for isomers, more branching (a rounder shape) lowers it.
w: Three choices are C5H12 isomers; the most branched, nearly spherical 2,2-dimethylpropane has the least surface contact and weakest dispersion forces: C(CH3)4 (about 10 °C, vs 36 °C for pentane). Hexane is larger, so it boils highest.

q: Propane, dimethyl ether and ethanol have similar molar masses. Which ranking of boiling points is correct?
h: With similar size, rank by the strongest IMF: dispersion only < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding.
w: Propane is nonpolar (dispersion only), dimethyl ether is polar (dipole–dipole), and ethanol has O–H (hydrogen bonding): propane < dimethyl ether < ethanol (−42 °C, −24 °C, 78 °C).

q: Which alkane has the strongest London dispersion forces and therefore the highest melting point?
h: Dispersion forces grow with molecular size (more electrons, more surface area).
w: The 20-carbon alkane is the biggest molecule, so it has the strongest dispersion forces and the highest melting point: CH3(CH2)18CH3. It is a waxy solid at room temperature, like the alkanes in petroleum jelly, while the others are liquids.

q: Which compound is the most soluble in water?
h: More –OH groups per carbon means more hydrogen bonding with water and a smaller nonpolar part.
w: Ethylene glycol has two –OH groups on only two carbons and mixes with water in all proportions: HOCH2CH2OH. 1-Butanol and diethyl ether dissolve only slightly (about 7 g per 100 mL); pentane is nonpolar and insoluble.

q: What is the shape around the oxygen atom in dimethyl ether, CH<sub>3</sub>–O–CH<sub>3</sub>, and the approximate C–O–C bond angle?
h: Count electron groups on O: two bonds plus two lone pairs.
w: Oxygen has 2 bonding groups and 2 lone pairs = 4 electron groups (tetrahedral arrangement), so the molecular shape is bent, about 109°, like water. Because it is bent, the C–O dipoles do not cancel and the ether is polar.

q: What is the shape and approximate bond angle around the carbonyl (C=O) carbon of acetone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Count electron groups on the carbonyl carbon; a double bond counts as one group.
w: The carbonyl carbon has three groups (two CH3 and one C=O) and no lone pairs: trigonal planar, 120°. The methyl carbons are tetrahedral, which is the tempting wrong answer.

q: Which molecule is nonpolar even though it contains polar bonds?
h: In a tetrahedral molecule, bond dipoles cancel only if all four atoms on carbon are identical.
w: In tetrachloromethane all four C–Cl dipoles point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron and cancel: CCl4. With a mix of H and Cl on carbon the dipoles do not cancel, so CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CH3Cl are polar.

q: Acetic acid reacts with methylamine as shown below. Which statement is correct?
c: CH<sub>3</sub>COOH is the acid; CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> is the base.
CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> is the acid; CH<sub>3</sub>COOH is the base.
Both CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> act as acids.
Both CH<sub>3</sub>COOH and CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> act as bases.
h: Follow the H<sup>+</sup>: the acid donates it, the base accepts it.
w: Acetic acid loses H+ (becoming acetate), and methylamine gains it (becoming methylammonium). Carboxylic acid = acid, amine = base.

q: In which reaction does water act as an acid?
h: Water is amphoteric. It acts as an acid when it gives H<sup>+</sup> away, leaving OH<sup>−</sup>.
w: With the amine (a base), water donates H+ and becomes OH−: CH3NH2 + H2O. With acids (HCl, carboxylic acids) water accepts H+ to form H3O+, so there it is a base.

q: Which pair contains a strong acid and a strong base?
h: Strong acids include HCl, HBr, HI, HNO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, HClO<sub>4</sub>; strong bases are group 1 hydroxides. Organic acids and amines are weak.
w: HCl and NaOH both ionize completely in water. Carboxylic acids such as acetic acid are weak acids, and amines and ammonia are weak bases.

q: Acetaminophen, the pain reliever in Tylenol, has the formula C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>. What is its molar mass?
h: Multiply each atomic mass by its subscript and add: C 12.01, H 1.008, N 14.01, O 16.00.
w: 8(12.01) + 9(1.008) + 1(14.01) + 2(16.00) = 96.08 + 9.072 + 14.01 + 32.00 = 151.16 g mol⁻¹. 43.03 comes from adding one of each atom without the subscripts; 135.16 uses only one O; 137.15 leaves out the nitrogen.

q: Lactic acid, which builds up in muscles during hard exercise, is CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)COOH. What is its molar mass?
h: First write the molecular formula, counting every H (including those on O) and every O, then add atomic masses.
w: Formula C3H6O3: 3(12.01) + 6(1.008) + 3(16.00) = 36.03 + 6.048 + 48.00 = 90.08 g mol⁻¹. Missing one H on an –OH gives 89.07; dropping one O (C3H6O2) gives 74.08.

q: Rank the compounds in the table, which have similar molar masses, from highest to lowest boiling point.
h: Same size, so compare the strongest attraction: H-bonding (and how many), dipole–dipole, or only London forces.
w: Carboxylic acids form two H-bonds per pair (dimers) → highest. Alcohols H-bond once. Propanal has dipole–dipole only, and butane only London forces: acetic acid > 1-propanol > propanal > butane. Putting the alcohol first underrates the acid's stronger H-bonding.

q: Lidocaine, C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>22</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O, is a dental anesthetic. What is its molar mass?
h: Multiply each atomic mass by its subscript and add: C 12.01, H 1.008, N 14.01, O 16.00.

q: A base that is 100% dissociated in aqueous solution is called strong. Pick the strong base.
h: Strong bases ionize completely in water. Group 1 hydroxides are the classic examples.
w: KOH dissociates completely into K+ and OH−, so it is a strong base. Ammonia, amines and carboxylate ions accept H+ only partially: they are weak bases.

q: Which compound's molecules attract each other ONLY through London dispersion forces?
h: Molecules with O or N are generally polar. Which choice contains only C and H?
w: Pentane has only C–H and C–C bonds, so it is nonpolar and has only London forces. The ether and aldehyde are polar (dipole–dipole), and the amine has N–H for hydrogen bonding.

q: Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line) between methanol and water?
h: A hydrogen bond needs an H that is bonded to O, N or F, pointing at a lone pair on another O, N or F.
w: Only the picture where the H of methanol's O–H points at the O of water is a hydrogen bond: a δ+ H on oxygen attracted to a lone pair on oxygen. The most tempting wrong picture uses an H from the CH3 group, but a C–H bond is almost nonpolar, so that H has no real δ+ charge. H···H and H···C lines have no lone pair to accept the H.

q: Acetone dissolves in water. Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line) between acetone and water?
h: Acetone has no O–H, so which molecule must supply the H? What on acetone can accept it?
w: Water supplies the H (bonded to O), and the lone pair on acetone's C=O oxygen accepts it. The tempting wrong pictures use an H from acetone's CH3 group, but H on carbon is not δ+ enough to hydrogen bond. A dotted line to the carbonyl carbon is wrong because carbon has no lone pair.

q: Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line)?
h: Check both ends of the dotted line: the H must be on N, O or F, and the other end must be an N, O or F atom.
w: The N–H of methylamine pointing at the oxygen of water is a hydrogen bond. The tempting N–H···CH3 picture has a good donor but a bad acceptor: a carbon has no lone pair and is not very electronegative. C–H···N fails at the donor end, and H···H has two δ+ atoms facing each other.

q: Trimethylamine, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N, is mixed with water. Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line)?
h: Trimethylamine has no N–H, but its N still has a lone pair. A hydrogen bond always has an H in the middle.
w: Water's O–H points at the lone pair on the nitrogen, so that is a hydrogen bond. A 3° amine cannot donate, but it can accept. The N···O picture has no H between the atoms, so it is not a hydrogen bond at all, and the CH3 pictures use H on carbon or a carbon acceptor.

q: Diethyl ether (ethoxyethane) is slightly soluble in water. Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line)?
h: Which molecule here has an H on oxygen? The ether can only take part through its oxygen's lone pairs.
w: Only water has an O–H, so water must be the donor: water's H pointing at the ether oxygen. The most tempting wrong picture shows two ether molecules joined C–H···O, but ethers have no O–H or N–H, so they cannot hydrogen bond to each other. A dotted line to a carbon of the ether is wrong because carbon has no lone pair.

q: Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line) between two molecules of the same compound?
h: For a compound to hydrogen bond to itself, each molecule needs an O–H or N–H, and the H must point at an O or N.
w: Ethanol O–H···O ethanol is correct: ethanol has an O–H (donor) and an O with lone pairs (acceptor). The tempting dimethyl ether picture uses an H on carbon, and ethers cannot hydrogen bond to themselves. O–H···H–O puts two δ+ H atoms together, and O–H···C points at a carbon with no lone pair.

q: In proteins, amide groups hold helices and sheets in shape by hydrogen bonding. Which picture shows a correct hydrogen bond (dotted line) between two acetamide molecules?
h: Amides have an N–H (donor) and a C=O (acceptor). Which atom of the C=O group has the lone pairs?
w: The N–H of one amide points at the C=O oxygen of the other, the same N–H···O=C link that holds protein helices and sheets together. The tempting wrong picture points the N–H at the carbonyl carbon, but the lone pairs are on the oxygen. C–H···O and N–H···H–N are not hydrogen bonds.

q: Methane and water are shown with a dotted line between them. Is the dotted line a hydrogen bond?
c: No. The H is bonded to carbon, and a C–H bond is not polar enough.
Yes. The H is pointing at a lone pair on the oxygen of water.
Yes. Any H atom near an O, N or F atom forms a hydrogen bond.
No. The oxygen of water cannot accept a hydrogen bond.
h: Look at what the H on the left is bonded to. Is that bond polar?
w: The acceptor (water's O) is fine, but the donor is not: C and H have nearly the same electronegativity, so the H has almost no δ+ charge. Not a hydrogen bond. The tempting "yes" answer only checks the acceptor end; both ends must be right. Water's O certainly can accept hydrogen bonds.

q: Water and acetaldehyde (ethanal) are shown with a dotted line between them. Is the dotted line a hydrogen bond?
c: Yes. An H on oxygen points at a lone pair on the C=O oxygen.
No. Acetaldehyde has no O–H, so it cannot take part in hydrogen bonding.
No. A hydrogen bond needs an O–H group on both molecules.
Yes. The H of water is attracted to the C=O carbon.
h: A hydrogen bond needs a donor (H on N, O or F) and an acceptor (lone pair on N, O or F). Do they have to be on different molecules?
w: Water donates its O–H hydrogen, and the lone pair on the aldehyde oxygen accepts it, so this is a hydrogen bond. The tempting "no" confuses the two jobs: aldehydes cannot hydrogen bond to each other (no O–H), but they can accept from water. That is why small aldehydes dissolve in water.

q: Dimethylamine and ethane are shown with a dotted line between them. Is the dotted line a hydrogen bond?
c: No. The H points at a carbon, which has no lone pair.
Yes. The H is bonded to N, so it is a hydrogen-bond donor.
No. Only H atoms bonded to oxygen can form hydrogen bonds.
Yes. The N–H hydrogen is δ+ and the carbon is δ−.
h: Check both ends of the dotted line, not just the H end.
w: The donor end is fine (H on N), but the other end is a CH3 carbon: no lone pair and not electronegative, so no hydrogen bond. The tempting "yes" only checks the donor. N–H hydrogens do hydrogen bond (to N, O or F), so "only O–H" is wrong.

q: Two ethanol molecules are shown with a dotted line between them. Is the dotted line a hydrogen bond?
c: No. Both ends are δ+ H atoms; the H must point at a lone pair on O, N or F.
Yes. Both H atoms are bonded to oxygen, so they attract each other.
No. Ethanol molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other.
Yes. Opposite partial charges on the two H atoms attract each other.
h: What partial charge does an H on oxygen carry? Would two of them attract?
w: Both H atoms are δ+, so they repel; a hydrogen bond joins a δ+ H to a lone pair on an electronegative atom. Not a hydrogen bond. Ethanol can hydrogen bond to itself, but the line would have to run from the O–H hydrogen of one molecule to the O of the other.

q: Water and N,N-dimethylethylamine (a 3° amine) are shown with a dotted line between them. Is the dotted line a hydrogen bond?
c: Yes. The H on oxygen points at the lone pair on the nitrogen.
No. A 3° amine has no N–H, so it cannot take part in hydrogen bonding.
No. Hydrogen bonds can form only between two oxygen atoms.
Yes. The N is bonded to three carbons, which makes it δ+.
h: A 3° amine cannot donate an H. Can it still accept one?
w: Water supplies the δ+ H, and the amine nitrogen still has a lone pair to accept it, so this is a hydrogen bond. The tempting "no" mixes up donating and accepting: a 3° amine cannot hydrogen bond to itself, but it does hydrogen bond with water, which is why small 3° amines are water-soluble.

q: Which compound can hydrogen bond to other molecules of itself in the pure liquid?
h: To hydrogen bond to itself, a molecule needs an H bonded directly to O or N.
w: 1-Propanol has an O–H, so one molecule's O–H hydrogen can point at another molecule's oxygen. Methoxyethane (an ether), propanal and propanone all have O atoms that could accept, but no O–H to donate, so between their own molecules the strongest attractions are dipole–dipole attractions. The most common mistake is counting any oxygen as enough.

q: Which compound can accept hydrogen bonds from water but cannot hydrogen bond to other molecules of itself?
h: Look for a molecule with an O or N lone pair but no H bonded to O or N.
w: Ethyl acetate (an ester) has oxygen lone pairs that accept H from water, but no O–H or N–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond to itself. Butanoic acid and butylamine have O–H or N–H, so they do hydrogen bond to themselves. Hexane has neither, so it cannot hydrogen bond even with water.

q: Which compound cannot form hydrogen bonds with water at all?
h: Water can donate its H to any O or N lone pair. Which molecule has no O or N?
w: Cyclohexane is only C and H, so it has no lone pair to accept water's H and no polar H to donate. The tempting wrong answers (cyclohexanone, diethyl ether, triethylamine) cannot hydrogen bond to themselves, but each has an O or N lone pair that accepts an H from water.

q: Pure samples of compounds I–IV are shown. In how many of them do the molecules hydrogen bond to each other?
h: For each one, ask: is there an H bonded directly to O or N?
w: 2: 1-butanol (I) has an O–H and butanamide (IV) has N–H bonds. Butanal (II) and diethyl ether (III) have oxygen lone pairs but no O–H or N–H, so they cannot hydrogen bond to themselves. Answering 1 usually means the amide N–H was missed; answering 3 or 4 means any oxygen was counted.

q: How many of the compounds I–IV can form hydrogen bonds with water?
h: Water can be the donor. Any O or N lone pair in the other molecule can accept water's H.
w: 3: diethyl ether (II), cyclohexanone (III) and 1-pentanol (IV) all have oxygen lone pairs that accept an H from water (the alcohol can also donate). Only pentane (I), with just C and H, cannot. Answering 1 is the common mistake of counting only molecules with an O–H.

q: Acetone (propanone), shown, mixes with water in all proportions. What is the main attraction between acetone and water molecules?
c: Water's O–H hydrogen bonds to the oxygen of acetone's C=O.
Acetone's C–H hydrogens hydrogen bond to water's oxygen.
Acetone molecules hydrogen bond to each other through their C=O.
The carbon of acetone's C=O accepts a hydrogen bond from water.
h: Acetone has no O–H. Which molecule donates the H, and which atom has lone pairs?
w: Water donates its δ+ H to a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen. Acetone's H atoms are all on carbon, so they cannot donate, and acetone cannot hydrogen bond to itself. The carbonyl carbon is δ+ and has no lone pair, so it cannot accept a hydrogen bond.

q: Ethanol (I) and dimethyl ether (II) have the same formula, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O. Ethanol boils at 78 °C, but dimethyl ether boils at −24 °C. Why?
c: Ethanol molecules hydrogen bond to each other; dimethyl ether has no O–H.
Ethanol has a larger molar mass, so its dispersion forces are stronger.
Boiling dimethyl ether breaks its weak C–O covalent bonds.
Dimethyl ether is nonpolar, so only London dispersion forces act.
h: Same formula means same molar mass. What does ethanol have that the ether lacks?
w: Ethanol's O–H lets its molecules hydrogen bond to each other, which takes much more energy to overcome. The two have identical molar masses (46.07 g mol⁻¹), so dispersion cannot explain it. Dimethyl ether is actually polar (bent C–O–C), so it has dipole–dipole attractions, just no hydrogen bonds. Boiling never breaks covalent bonds.

q: Phenol (I) boils at about 182 °C, but anisole (methoxybenzene, II) boils at about 154 °C. Which statement best explains this?
c: Phenol has an O–H, so its molecules hydrogen bond to each other; anisole cannot.
Phenol has the larger molar mass, so its London dispersion forces are stronger.
Anisole is nonpolar, so only London dispersion forces act between its molecules.
Only phenol has an aromatic ring, which raises the boiling point.
h: Anisole is phenol with the H on oxygen replaced by CH<sub>3</sub>. What does that remove?
w: Replacing the O–H hydrogen with CH3 removes the hydrogen-bond donor, so anisole molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other and anisole boils lower. Molar mass points the other way (anisole 108.13 g mol⁻¹ vs phenol 94.11 g mol⁻¹). Anisole is still polar (dipole–dipole), and both compounds have a benzene ring.

q: Which hydrocarbon has the strongest London dispersion forces between its molecules?
h: Dispersion forces grow with the number of electrons, so compare the size of the molecules.
w: Nonane (C9H20) is the largest molecule, with the most electrons and the most surface contact, so it has the strongest dispersion forces (bp 151 °C). Hexane, cyclopentane and 2-methylbutane are smaller. Being a ring or a branched chain does not make up for having fewer carbons.

q: All four alkanes shown are isomers of C8H18. Which has the highest boiling point?
h: Same formula means the same number of electrons. Which shape gives the most contact between neighboring molecules?
w: Unbranched octane (bp 126 °C) is long and can lie alongside its neighbors, giving the most surface contact and the strongest London dispersion forces. Branching makes molecules more compact, so 2,3,4-trimethylpentane (114 °C), 2,5-dimethylhexane (109 °C) and 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (99 °C) boil lower. Same molar mass does not mean same boiling point.

q: All four alkanes shown are isomers of C6H14. Which has the lowest boiling point?
h: More branching makes a molecule more compact (closer to a ball). How does that affect contact between molecules?
w: 2,2-Dimethylbutane is the most branched and most compact, so it has the least surface contact and the weakest London dispersion forces (bp 50 °C). Hexane is the highest (69 °C). The tempting choice, hexane, is the opposite trend: long unbranched chains boil highest.

q: Rank alkanes I–IV from highest to lowest boiling point.
h: First compare size (number of carbons). For the isomers with the same size, less branching means a higher boiling point.
w: Hexane (II, six carbons) is largest: 69 °C. The other three are C5H12 isomers: unbranched pentane (IV, 36 °C) > 2-methylbutane (I, 28 °C) > the very compact 2,2-dimethylpropane (III, 9.5 °C). So II > IV > I > III. Putting III high reverses the branching rule.

q: Pentane (I) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (II) are both C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. Which statement is correct?
c: Pentane boils higher: its long shape gives more contact and stronger dispersion forces.
2,2-Dimethylpropane boils higher: its compact shape packs its electrons closer together.
They boil at the same temperature because they have the same molar mass.
Pentane boils higher because its molecules hydrogen bond to each other.
h: Both are nonpolar, so only London dispersion forces act. Which shape lets molecules touch over more area?
w: Rod-shaped pentane molecules lie alongside each other and touch over a large area, so pentane has stronger dispersion forces and boils higher (36 °C vs 9.5 °C). Same molar mass does not guarantee the same boiling point; shape matters. Neither compound has an O–H or N–H, so there is no hydrogen bonding.

q: Which compound is the most soluble in water?
h: Water dissolves small molecules that can hydrogen bond (–OH, –COOH, –NH<sub>2</sub>, C=O). Which group hydrogen bonds most strongly?
w: Butanoic acid mixes with water in all proportions: its –COOH group has both a C=O and an O–H, so it accepts and donates hydrogen bonds to water. 1-Butanol (about 77 g L⁻¹) and butanal (about 71 g L⁻¹) are only partly soluble. Butane has no O or N and is nearly insoluble.

q: Which compound is the least soluble in water?
h: Which molecule has nothing that can hydrogen bond with water?
w: Hexane has only C and H; it is nonpolar and cannot hydrogen bond with water, so it is essentially insoluble. 1-Hexanol, hexanoic acid and hexylamine each have a polar group that hydrogen bonds with water (all three are slightly soluble, about 6–12 g L⁻¹), even though their six-carbon chains limit how much dissolves.

q: Rank alcohols I–IV from most to least soluble in water.
h: All have one –OH. What happens to solubility as the nonpolar carbon chain gets longer?
w: Each has one –OH that hydrogen bonds with water, but the nonpolar chain gets longer from methanol (II, miscible) to 1-butanol (IV, about 77 g L⁻¹) to 1-hexanol (I, about 6 g L⁻¹) to 1-octanol (III, about 0.5 g L⁻¹). So II > IV > I > III. The reverse order comes from thinking bigger molecules have "more" to attract water; only the –OH does.

q: All four compounds have five carbons. Which is the most soluble in water?
h: With the same chain length, more groups that hydrogen bond with water means higher solubility.
w: 1,5-Pentanediol has two –OH groups, one at each end, so it hydrogen bonds with water strongly enough to mix in all proportions. 1-Pentanol, with one –OH, dissolves only about 22 g L⁻¹; pentanal (one C=O, no O–H) about 12 g L⁻¹; pentane is insoluble. More polar groups on the same chain beat one polar group.

q: Rank compounds I–IV from most to least soluble in water.
h: First: which compounds can hydrogen bond with water at all? Then compare chain lengths among those that can.
w: The three alcohols hydrogen bond with water, and the shorter the chain the better: ethanol (III, miscible) > 1-butanol (IV, about 77 g L⁻¹) > 1-hexanol (I, about 6 g L⁻¹). Hexane (II) cannot hydrogen bond and is nearly insoluble: III > IV > I > II. Ranking IV above III assumes a bigger alcohol dissolves better; the extra CH2 groups are nonpolar.

q: 1-Octanol, shown, has an –OH group but is almost insoluble in water (about 0.5 g L⁻¹). Why?
c: Its long nonpolar carbon chain outweighs the one polar –OH group.
Its –OH group cannot hydrogen bond with water because it is at the end of the chain.
Alcohols with more than five carbons lose their –OH group in water.
Its molar mass is too large for any molecule to dissolve in water.
h: Think of the molecule as two parts: a polar "head" and a nonpolar "tail." Which part is bigger here?
w: The –OH does hydrogen bond with water, but the 8-carbon chain is nonpolar and must push water molecules apart without forming hydrogen bonds. The large nonpolar part dominates, so 1-octanol barely dissolves. The –OH works fine at the end of a chain (methanol and ethanol mix completely), and size alone is not the issue: glucose (180 g mol⁻¹) dissolves easily.

q: Which compound is the most soluble in water?
h: Which molecule has an H on N or O and a lone pair to share with water? Thiols (–SH) and alkyl halides hydrogen bond very weakly.
w: Propylamine mixes with water in all proportions: its –NH2 both donates and accepts hydrogen bonds. 1-Chloropropane (about 2.7 g L⁻¹) and 1-propanethiol (about 1.9 g L⁻¹) are only slightly soluble because S and Cl do not form useful hydrogen bonds; the –SH looks like –OH but sulfur is not electronegative enough. Butane is nearly insoluble.

q: Cholesterol, shown, is found in every cell membrane. How is cholesterol best described?
c: Mostly nonpolar: one –OH on a big hydrocarbon frame, so it is fat-soluble.
Mostly polar: its –OH group makes the whole molecule dissolve easily in water.
Mostly polar: its four rings and C=C bond carry partial charges.
Ionic: the –OH group gives the molecule a negative charge in blood.
h: Compare the size of the polar part with the size of the C–H part.
w: Cholesterol (C27H46O) has one –OH on 27 carbons, so it is mostly nonpolar and fat-soluble; that is why it travels in blood inside lipoproteins. The one –OH makes only one end slightly polar, so cholesterol sits in membranes with its OH facing the water. One polar group cannot carry a molecule this large into water.

q: Vitamin C (I) is water-soluble, but vitamin A (retinol, II) is fat-soluble. Which statement best explains the difference?
c: Vitamin C has four –OH groups on six carbons; vitamin A has one –OH on 20.
Vitamin A has no oxygen atoms, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water at all.
Vitamin C has the larger molar mass, so it attracts more water molecules.
Vitamin A's C=C double bonds are polar, so they repel water.
h: Count the –OH groups in each and compare them with the number of carbons.
w: Vitamin C (C6H8O6) has four –OH groups and two more O atoms on only six carbons, so it hydrogen bonds extensively with water. Retinol (C20H30O) has a single –OH at the end of a 20-carbon hydrocarbon, so the nonpolar part wins. Retinol does have an O, and it is actually heavier (286 vs 176 g mol⁻¹); C=C bonds are nonpolar.

q: Vitamins I–IV are shown (II is a form of vitamin K). Which one is water-soluble?
h: Water-soluble vitamins have several groups that hydrogen bond with water on a small carbon frame.
w: III is vitamin B6 (pyridoxine): three –OH groups and a ring N on only eight carbons, so it hydrogen bonds well with water. I (vitamin A, retinol), II (menadione, vitamin K) and IV (vitamin D3) are mostly hydrocarbon, with at most one –OH or two C=O groups on a large nonpolar frame, so they are fat-soluble. The tempting choice I has an –OH, but one –OH is not enough for a 20-carbon molecule.

q: Estradiol, shown, is the main estrogen hormone. Which labeled carbon is bonded to a polar group that can hydrogen bond with water?
h: Polar regions contain O or N bonded to H. A carbon bonded only to C and H atoms is in a nonpolar region.
w: Carbon c carries the phenol –OH, whose O–H can donate and whose O can accept hydrogen bonds. Carbons a, b and d are bonded only to C and H (ring-fusion carbon, methyl group, ring C–H), so they are in nonpolar regions; the tempting d is in the same ring as the –OH but bonded only to C and H. Estradiol has only two –OH groups on 18 carbons, so it is mostly nonpolar and passes easily through cell membranes.

q: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), shown, is only slightly soluble in water. Which part of the molecule can hydrogen bond with water?
c: the CH<sub>3</sub> next to the –COOH group
h: Hydrogen bonding with water needs O or N atoms. Where are the O atoms?
w: Only the –COOH group has O atoms: its O–H donates and both oxygens accept hydrogen bonds. The benzene ring, the isobutyl group and the CH3 are all hydrocarbon and nonpolar. Because 12 of its 13 carbons are in nonpolar parts and only one group is polar, ibuprofen dissolves poorly in water (about 0.02 g L⁻¹).

q: Acetaminophen (Tylenol), shown, has the formula C8H9NO2. How many of its hydrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond donors?
h: A donor H must be bonded directly to N, O or F. Find every O–H and N–H.
w: Acetaminophen has one O–H (the phenol) and one N–H (the amide), so 2 donor H atoms. The other seven H atoms are on carbon. Answering 1 misses the amide N–H; answering 9 counts every H in the formula. The C=O oxygen is an acceptor, not a donor.

q: Albuterol, shown, is the drug in rescue inhalers for asthma. How many of its hydrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond donors?
h: Count every H bonded to O or N. Look at each O and the N carefully, including the one between carbons.
w: Albuterol has three –OH groups (a phenol, a CH2OH and a secondary alcohol) and one N–H (a 2° amine): 4 donor H atoms. Answering 3 misses the N–H, which is easy to overlook because the N sits in the middle of the chain. The tert-butyl group has only C–H bonds.

q: Propofol, shown, is an IV anesthetic. It is so insoluble in water that it is given as a milky oil-in-water emulsion. What feature of its structure explains this?
c: Its one –OH is surrounded by a benzene ring and two isopropyl groups.
It has no O or N atoms, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water at all.
Its –OH group makes it ionic, and ionic compounds do not dissolve in water.
Its molar mass is over 1000 g mol⁻¹, too large to dissolve in water.
h: Find the one polar group and compare it with the size of the hydrocarbon part around it.
w: Propofol (C12H18O) has a single –OH on a 12-carbon hydrocarbon, and the two bulky isopropyl groups crowd around it, so the molecule is mostly nonpolar. It does have an oxygen that can hydrogen bond, so "no O or N" is wrong. It is a neutral molecule (not ionic), and its molar mass is only 178.3 g mol⁻¹.

q: Acetaminophen (I) dissolves in water at about 14 g L⁻¹, while ibuprofen (II) dissolves at only about 0.02 g L⁻¹. Which explanation fits their structures?
c: I has two polar groups on 8 carbons; II has one polar group on 13 carbons.
II is less soluble because only I contains a benzene ring.
II's –COOH is less polar than any group in I, so II cannot hydrogen bond with water.
I is more soluble because it is the larger molecule, with more atoms to attract water.
h: Count the polar groups in each, then count carbons. Which has more polar groups per carbon?
w: Acetaminophen has two polar groups (phenol O–H and amide N–H/C=O) on 8 carbons; ibuprofen has one –COOH on 13 carbons, so its nonpolar part dominates. Both molecules have a benzene ring, and ibuprofen's –COOH does hydrogen bond with water; it just cannot outweigh the large hydrocarbon part. Acetaminophen is the smaller molecule.

q: Chemists call water amphoteric. Which statement explains the term?
c: It can act as either a proton donor (acid) or a proton acceptor (base), depending on its partner.
It is a strong acid and a strong base at the same time, so it neutralizes itself completely.
It can neither donate nor accept protons, so any solution made with it stays exactly neutral.
It dissolves polar and nonpolar substances equally well, so it is called a universal solvent.
h: Think about what water does with HCl versus what it does with an amine.
w: With an acid such as HCl, water accepts H+ (acts as a base, forming H3O+); with a base such as CH3NH2, water donates H+ (acts as an acid, forming OH−). Either role, depending on the partner, is what amphoteric means. Water is a weak acid and a weak base, not strong, and its solvent behavior is a separate idea.

q: Propanoic acid ionizes in water as written below. What role does water play here?
c: a base, because it accepts a proton from the carboxylic acid
an acid, because it donates a proton to the carboxylic acid
a base, because it donates a proton to the carboxylic acid
an acid, because it accepts a proton from the carboxylic acid
h: Follow the H<sup>+</sup>: whatever gains it is the base; whatever loses it is the acid.
w: Propanoic acid loses H+ (acid → propanoate ion) and water gains it, becoming H3O+. A species that accepts a proton is a base, so here water is the base. Bases never donate protons, and water accepting a proton makes it a base, not an acid.

q: One of the following acids ionizes completely in water (a strong acid). Which one?
h: Only a short list of inorganic acids ionize completely. Carboxylic acids never do.
w: HBr (like HCl, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, HClO4) ionizes essentially 100% in water, so it is strong. Propanoic acid and benzoic acid are carboxylic acids: organic acids are weak. HF is the tempting one: it is a hydrogen halide, but it is a weak acid, unlike HCl, HBr and HI.

q: Three of these bases dissociate completely in water; one does not. Which is the weak base?
h: Metal hydroxides of Groups 1 and 2 dissociate completely. What kind of base is an amine?
w: Ethylamine is an organic base: it accepts H+ from water only partly (CH3CH2NH2 + H2O ⇌ CH3CH2NH+3 + OH−), so it is weak. NaOH, KOH and Ca(OH)2 are ionic hydroxides that dissociate completely: strong bases.

q: Each drawn compound has a six-carbon chain, so their dispersion forces are about equal. Which one melts at the highest temperature?
h: Same size means similar dispersion forces, so compare the other forces: which compound can form the most hydrogen bonds?
w: Hexanoic acid has an O–H donor and two oxygens; its molecules pair up through two hydrogen bonds each, giving the strongest attractions and the highest melting point (about −3 °C). 1-Hexanol can hydrogen bond, but only one O–H per molecule (−47 °C); hexanal has a polar C=O but no O–H (−56 °C); hexane has only dispersion forces (−95 °C). The same ranking applies to boiling points.

q: Oil of wintergreen (methyl salicylate), drawn below, gives muscle rubs their warming smell. Count its atoms and use the table to find the molar mass.
h: Each corner or line end is a carbon with enough H to make four bonds. Count C, H and O, then multiply by the atomic masses.
w: The formula is C8H8O3: 8(12.01) + 8(1.008) + 3(16.00) = 96.08 + 8.06 + 48.00 = 152.14 g mol−1. Forgetting the four hidden H atoms on the ring gives 148.11; missing one oxygen gives 136.14; doubling the H count gives 160.21.
